$comment: Corrections applied on top of the reference gir files. 'skip' removes symbols from generation - a callable by c:identifier, a type by its qualified gir name, a property by its GObject spelling -, 'forceOpaque' keeps a record behind a pointer instead of copying it by value, 'rename' overrides the derived C# name, 'annotationOverrides' patches wrong or missing transfer/nullable/array annotations and states the facts about a C function that no gir annotation carries - the 'direction' of a pointer to a plain structure, to a GValue, to a scalar, to an enumeration or to a record the function works on in place, and the 'fixedArraySize' of a caller allocated out array and the 'scope' of a callback parameter the library keeps longer than the gir says; a signal argument is addressed by the GObject spelling of its signal, 'GES.Project::error-loading-asset#error', where only 'nullable' is read; on the bare identifier of a callable it may also state 'obsolete', the message of an [Obsolete] attribute the emitted member carries; 'arrayOverrides' corrects the length, the fixed size, the zero termination or the element type of an <array> the gir already spells, 'returnTypeOverrides' narrows a returned handle onto the type that declares the member.
$comment-skip-static-str: The *_static_str family stores the string the caller passes by pointer and never copies it, so the string has to outlive every use of the object it was stored in. The generated marshalling hands native code a stack or heap buffer that is released when the call returns, which leaves the library holding a dangling pointer for every string that does not fit the short string optimisation. The gir carries no annotation that says a string must be static, so there is nothing for the planner to key on and the symbols are listed here. Binding them needs hand written glue that hands over an interned copy. The three *_value_static_str entries are the same family for the field name string of a value write: gstidstr-private.h:130-132 inline-copies a name of at most 15 bytes and aliases the caller's pointer beyond that, a silent, length dependent dangling hazard. gst_structure_take_value_static_str would also be rejected as a consuming take_value; it is listed here with the static-str rationale so that a future take-value emission cannot bind it either.
$comment-skip-identity: gst_buffer_remove_meta is hand bound as Gst.Buffer.RemoveMeta. The identity fault this entry was first written for is gone - '$comment-force-opaque-meta' keeps GstMeta behind a pointer, so the call is handed the address the buffer handed out - and what kept it out afterwards was the other end: removing a metadata item frees it synchronously (gstbuffer.c:gst_buffer_remove_meta unlinks, calls info->free_func and g_frees the item before it returns), and the wrapper the caller passed in is a bare pointer holder that nothing invalidates. That is what the hand written member adds and no emission shape expresses: it zeroes the wrapper's handle when, and only when, the call answers TRUE, because every FALSE path (not writable, GST_META_FLAG_LOCKED, a meta of another buffer) leaves the item alive. Gst.Buffer.ForeachMeta applies the same convention to the item a callback asks to remove.
$comment-skip-annotations: These five functions carry annotations that do not describe what the C function does, and following them produces wrong lengths or wrong ownership: gst_adapter_map returns a pointer whose length is the size argument rather than an annotated array, gst_adapter_take returns freshly allocated memory of the size argument, gst_type_find_peek returns a borrowed pointer of the size argument, and gst_audio_ring_buffer_commit both reads and writes its sample count while its data pointer carries no length at all. An annotation override cannot add a missing array length, so they are skipped.
$comment-skip-sample-count: gst_audio_ring_buffer_read is the same family as gst_audio_ring_buffer_commit above, with the twist that its annotation is present and reads as correct. Its data array is annotated with the len parameter as its length, but len counts samples while the array counts bytes, and the C function writes bytes_per_frame bytes for each sample it is asked for. The emitted call took the byte length of the span for the sample count, so every format wider than one byte per frame - which is every format an application actually uses, S16LE stereo being four - had the library write bytes_per_frame times past the end of the caller's memory. No annotation states the unit of a length, so there is nothing for the planner to key on. The call is bound in Gst.Audio.AudioRingBuffer.Read instead, with the same signature, where the span is measured in samples before it is handed over.
$comment-skip-consumed: gst_meta_info_register consumes the GstMetaInfo it is given and returns the registered one. The wrapper of an opaque record owns nothing and is never disposed, so nothing is freed twice, but the instance the caller still holds points at released memory the moment the call returns.
$comment-skip-superseded: gst_adapter_unmap releases what gst_adapter_map handed out, and gst_adapter_map is skipped just above. Emitting the release on its own leaves a public Unmap() with no Map() to pair it with, which unmaps a mapping the caller never took and releases a second time the one that the hand written scope holds. The mapping surface of an adapter is Gst.Base.Adapter.Map and the scope it returns, so this entry point is bound there and nowhere else.
$comment-skip-sync-handler: gst_bus_set_sync_handler installs a callback whose return value decides who owns the message: GST_BUS_DROP makes the handler responsible for unreffing it, every other reply leaves that to gst_bus_post. No annotation of the gir states a transfer that a return value turns on, so the generated marshalling cannot express it, and the emitted call had two faults because of it. It refused a null handler, which made the documented clear form unreachable and left a consumer unable to take the handler off at teardown; and its trampoline handed the managed handler a borrowed wrapper, so a handler that answered Drop leaked the reference of the poster with no way of consuming it from managed code. Both are fixed in Gst.Bus.SetSyncHandler and Gst.Bus.ClearSyncHandler, whose hand written trampoline drops that reference itself when the handler answers Drop. The delegate is hand written next to the install so that its documentation can state the contract the binding actually implements. Skipping the call no longer retires the generated GstBusSyncHandler on its own, because a hand bound consumer keeps its callback type generated; the type entry on the skip list is what does, see $comment-skip-hand-written-callback-types.
$comment-skip-deinit: ges_deinit releases everything ges_init built, and the editing services are unusable until another ges_init. The binding runs ges_init from GstGES.Initialize, behind a latch that says it has run, and nothing in the library tells that latch when the resources are gone: a caller who takes the shut down of the process into their own hands leaves the entry point of the module reporting an initialised GES that no longer exists, and no call can bring it back. This is the shape gst_adapter_unmap has, a release with no acquisition of its own to pair with, and the same answer. Deinitialising GES is what ending the process does, which the documentation of the C function says as well.
$comment-skip-unpaired: gst_adapter_unmap releases a mapping this binding has no way of taking: gst_adapter_map is hand bound behind Gst.Base.Adapter.Map, whose scope performs the release, so every call Unmap() could receive would unmap a mapping the caller never took. The audio and video counterparts used to be listed here for the same reason and are now owned by their own scopes, see $comment-skip-scope-owned.
$comment-skip-credentials: gst_rtsp_auth_credentials_free frees a NULL terminated array of GstRTSPAuthCredential, and the gir spells its parameter as a bare 'GstRTSPAuthCredential**' with no array element on it. The planner reads that as one handle, so the emitted call hands the library the address of a single credential and the loop inside the C function walks past it and frees whatever the words that follow happen to point at. No caller could get it right either: the only producer of such an array is gst_rtsp_message_parse_auth_credentials, whose out array is unannotated in the same way and which is skipped for it, so what a caller can hold is one GstRTSPAuthCredential. That one is a boxed wrapper which frees its own copy when it is disposed, which makes the call a double free on top of the walk. Binding the array needs an annotation the gir does not carry and glue that owns the whole block, and there is nothing to own while the parse call is unbound.
$comment-skip-watch: GstRTSPWatch is an asynchronous RTSP connection driven from a GLib main context, and nothing in the binding can produce one. gst_rtsp_watch_new is introspectable='0', because its funcs parameter is a table of nine callbacks and its notify parameter is a bare GDestroyNotify, so the gir describes no way of calling it and no overlay can bring it back; gst_rtsp_watch_attach takes a GLib.MainContext, which is not bound either. What is emitted is therefore a public class with seven methods, an internal constructor and no producer whatsoever: every one of Reset, SendMessage, SetFlushing, SetSendBacklog, GetSendBacklog, WaitBacklogUsec and Unref is unreachable by construction, and Unref is the same unpaired release that gst_adapter_unmap is. GstRTSPWatchFuncs is the callback table of that call and nothing else; its nine fields are all callback slots, so the record is emitted as a public class with no member at all. Both are skipped rather than shipped as a dead surface a consumer would have to discover is dead. The supported way of driving a connection is Gst.Rtsp.RTSPConnection and its fully bound *Usec calls, which are synchronous and need no main context. Reviving the watch needs a hand written GstRTSPWatchFuncs of unmanaged function pointers and glue that owns the callback state for the lifetime of the watch, and the surface belongs to that glue once it is written.
$comment-skip-hand-bound-consumers: The fifteen consuming calls that shipped in 1.28.2 as hand written members, from before the generator learned the consuming argument kind. The generator now emits the same contract - mint a value for the callee, dispose the wrapper, unconditionally - but the hand written members stay canonical: they carry documentation the generator cannot author (what the call is for, worked examples, the bus and preroll behaviour around it), and emitting them again would declare the same member twice in one class. One way to do it: the entry points stay on the skip ledger under OverlaySkip and the hand written surface is the binding.
$comment-skip-hand-bound-values: The GValue carrying calls that shipped in 1.28.2 as hand written members, from before the planner learned the GValue projection. The generator now emits the shapes - in/ref/out over the caller's own storage, a copy or an adoption on return - but the hand written members stay canonical: they carry documentation and typing the generator cannot author (the copy-out doctrine of Structure.GetValue, the writability guard of Structure.SetValue, the typed Iterator.Items<T> that gst_iterator_next's out value backs, the ValueOrder enumeration of Global.ValueCompare over gst_value_compare, the null contract of Global.ValueSerialize over gst_value_serialize, the tag list value accessors, the GES child property family), and emitting them again would declare the same member twice in one class. Same one-way-to-do-it rule as $comment-skip-hand-bound-consumers: the entry points stay on the skip ledger under OverlaySkip and the hand written surface is the binding. gst_iterator_next is listed for its own reason on top - its out caller-allocates value would now auto-bind beside Iterator.Items<T>, and a raw Next(out Value) invites reading an iterator the typed enumerable already drives.
$comment-skip-allocator-free: gst_allocator_free is the terminal destructor of a GstMemory: it dispatches to the free function of the allocator without reading the reference count, because it is the call the mini object dispose path makes once the count has reached zero. The consuming recipe assumes the callee releases or keeps the reference it is minted - every other consuming callee unrefs it or stores it - and this one destroys the object instead, so the reference the wrapper still owns would be released on freed memory. Nothing is lost by the skip: freeing a memory block is what disposing its wrapper already does, through the unref that respects the count.
$comment-skip-toc-append: gst_toc_append_entry and gst_toc_entry_append_sub_entry consume the entry they are given and open with g_return_if_fail (gst_mini_object_is_writable (entry)) on that same argument (gsttoc.c:237 and :675). A GstTocEntry is not LOCKABLE, so writable means a reference count of exactly one, and the reference the consuming recipe mints for the callee makes the count two by construction: the check can never pass. Every call raises a GLib CRITICAL, the entry is never appended - silent data loss - and the minted reference is never consumed, so it leaks on top. A callee that asserts writability on its consumed argument is incompatible with the mint-and-dispose recipe; binding the pair needs an emission variant that hands over the wrapper's own reference instead of minting one, which does not exist.
$comment-skip-release-buffer: gst_buffer_pool_release_buffer hands the last reference of a buffer back to its pool, and everything on that path keys on the reference being the last. A buffer that fails gst_buffer_is_all_memory_writable is discarded instead of requeued, and the reset that follows runs gst_buffer_resize and metadata removal, which assert writability themselves. With the reference the wrapper still holds across the call the count is never one, so every released buffer is discarded - recycling defeated, and a pool with a fixed number of slots starves - while the reset assertions raise CRITICALs on every call, which are fatal under G_DEBUG=fatal-criticals. The member the recipe can emit is therefore not unsafe so much as useless, and it is skipped for the same missing variant as the toc pair above: releasing a buffer usefully needs the wrapper's own reference stolen, not a minted one. Nothing is lost by the skip, because disposing the wrapper is the release - the final unref runs the pool's release path with the count at exactly one, which is how every buffer a pool hands out already goes back.
$comment-skip-rtsp-range: gst_rtsp_range_parse allocates a GstRTSPTimeRange on the heap and hands the pointer out, and gst_rtsp_range_free is the release that matches it. GstRTSPTimeRange has no GType and is projected as a by-value C# struct, so nothing on the managed side can carry the heap identity the pair is about: the out parameter of parse would have to copy the structure out and free the original, which is a shape the planner does not have, and free would then be handed the address of a copy that was never allocated. Binding either half alone is worse than binding neither - a parse whose result is never freed leaks once per call, and a free that is reachable from a value the caller built on the stack is a heap corruption a caller cannot see coming. The other three functions of the record take the range by value or by reference and are bound, so what is lost is the string parser alone; gst_rtsp_range_to_string is the direction that works. Reversing this needs a projection for a heap allocated plain structure, which is a decision of its own and not one this entry makes.
$comment-skip-cursors: GstByteReader, GstByteWriter, GstBitReader and GstBitWriter are cursors over a block of memory the caller already owns, and that surface is what .NET is built around. The block is a Span<byte>, System.Buffers.Binary.BinaryPrimitives reads and writes every width in either endianness as a single inlined instruction, and System.Buffers.ArrayBufferWriter<byte> is the growing writer, where a bound cursor would cross the P/Invoke boundary once per field. The memory is already reached as a span: Gst.Buffer.Map and Gst.Base.Adapter.Map hand one out and Gst.Buffer.NewMemdup takes one back, and the one search a span cannot express on its own - the masked 32 bit start code scan, which also crosses memory an adapter holds in discontiguous pieces - is bound on Gst.Base.Adapter.MaskedScanUint32. What the bit cursors add over the byte ones is a position measured in bits with fixed width reads and nothing else; no Exp-Golomb reader appears anywhere in the girs, so they answer no codec parsing case either. What would be emitted for the four is why they are listed here rather than left alone: the record emitter binds the methods declared on a plain structure as members over a pinned instance, so leaving the four alone would offer the 140 methods they declare in GstBase-1.0.gir - 16 on GstBitReader, 19 on GstBitWriter, 66 on GstByteReader and 39 on GstByteWriter - plus the eight new and new_with_* producers that go with them, at one crossing of the P/Invoke boundary per field. Skipping them as whole types is what keeps every one of those methods out - none of them is planned, so none of them is listed in skip-report.md either. Before the emitter learned that shape the same listing held back the opposite one and the same dead end, four public value types of raw fields with no member and no producer whatsoever, which is the dead surface GstRtsp.RTSPWatch is skipped for. The listing is what pins the decision in both directions: an emitter that learns to bind a shape it used to drop decides no scope of its own here, which is what binding those 140 cursor methods with nobody deciding to would have been. Reversing it is one forceOpaque entry, which is purely additive and can be made at any point in 1.28.x.
$comment-skip-unique-list-prepend: gst_value_unique_list_prepend_value cannot work in 1.28. It delegates straight to gst_value_list_prepend_value (gstvalue.c:1180-1186), whose first statement is g_return_if_fail (GST_VALUE_HOLDS_LIST (value)) - a check for GST_TYPE_LIST exactly, which a GST_TYPE_UNIQUE_LIST value never satisfies (gstvalue.c:751). Every call is therefore a GLib CRITICAL and a no-op, whatever the caller passes. Binding it would freeze a member that can only fail, so it is skipped and goes on the upstream report backlog instead; unskipping it once the guard is fixed is purely additive. The append and concat members of the same type are unaffected: they have implementations of their own.
$comment-skip-flagset-register: gst_flagset_register is the only function of a fundamental type that is not one of the three value containers item 14 binds, and it is not a container function at all: it registers a pretty-printing sub-class of GST_TYPE_FLAG_SET. Emitting it would add a public Gst.FlagSet holder that nobody designed, on the mechanism that was frozen for the containers, so it is skipped here to keep the surface to what was reviewed. The skip is what makes it visible: before the fundamental holder existed the whole class was dropped before the census saw it, so the function appeared nowhere at all. Unskipping it is one line and purely additive.
$comment-skip-scope-owned: gst_video_frame_unmap and gst_audio_buffer_unmap are the release half of a mapping the binding now takes: Gst.Video.VideoFrame.MapScope and Gst.Audio.AudioBuffer.MapScope own the GstVideoFrame and the GstAudioBuffer they were filled into and unmap it when they are disposed. The mapping travels with the scope and never with the wrapper, so a public Unmap() on the wrapper would release a mapping the wrapper does not own - Gst.Video.VideoAggregatorPad.GetPreparedFrame hands out a frame the aggregator still owns and unmaps itself, which makes that a double unmap by construction. Mapping is bound by the scopes named above; the release belongs to them and is one way, the convention the doc block of BufferNative.cs states.
$comment-skip-hand-bound-storage: Six entry points whose out parameter is storage the caller allocates and whose binding is hand written, so that the generated marshalling does not declare them a second time. gst_video_frame_map, gst_video_frame_map_id and gst_audio_buffer_map fill a mapping that has to be released again, which is a scope and not an out parameter; they are Gst.Video.VideoFrame.Map, .MapId and Gst.Audio.AudioBuffer.Map. gst_buffer_extract copies into a caller provided byte array, which is a Span destination rather than an allocation, and is Gst.Buffer.Extract. gst_query_parse_nth_allocation_param is void and leaves both of its out parameters untouched when the index is out of range, so the hand written Gst.Query.ParseNthAllocationParam range checks first and throws. gst_rtsp_transport_parse fills a GstRTSPTransport that is freed with gst_rtsp_transport_free rather than through a boxed free, so Gst.Rtsp.RTSPTransport.Parse allocates with gst_rtsp_transport_new and releases the same way.
$comment-skip-storage-siblings: Twelve entry points whose whole job is to initialise or parse into storage the caller allocates, each of which the binding already reaches through a sibling that allocates the record itself: gst_video_info_new and gst_video_info_new_from_caps, gst_video_info_dma_drm_new and gst_video_info_dma_drm_new_from_caps, gst_audio_info_new and gst_audio_info_new_from_caps, gst_dsd_info_new and gst_dsd_info_new_from_caps, gst_rtsp_transport_new, gst_sdp_message_new and gst_sdp_media_new. Binding the init and from_caps halves as well would add API parity and no reach, and every one of them would hand the caller a second way of producing the same value. gst_video_blend_scale_linear_RGBA is listed here for a different reason: its dest_buffer out parameter is left unwritten on several of its paths, so a caller cannot tell a produced buffer from an untouched one, and its own documentation declares the function bound for deprecation.
$comment-skip-hand-bound-callbacks: Four calls whose managed state has a lifetime no generated shape can express, written by hand instead. gst_buffer_new_wrapped_full and gst_memory_new_wrapped wrap memory the caller keeps: the gir calls data an (array length=size) of guint8, which is upstream's own doc comment (gstbuffer.c:991, gstallocator.c:649) and wrong twice over - the block is maxsize bytes, not size, and it must outlive the call, so no span or pinned array can stand for it - and both open with g_return_val_if_fail guards (gstallocator.c:671-672) whose NULL return gst_buffer_new_wrapped_full hands to gst_memory_lock unchecked, so the binding validates before it allocates anything. gst_install_plugins_async invokes its callback exactly once when it returns GST_INSTALL_PLUGINS_STARTED_OK and never otherwise (install-plugins.c:660-689, the child watch is registered only on that branch), so the state is freed at the call site on every other return - a condition no generic emission keys on, and the common one on Windows, where the helper is absent. gst_video_codec_frame_set_user_data runs the previous notify synchronously when it is replaced (gstvideoutils.c:77-85) and stores the GCHandle in the user_data slot the frame carries, so Gst.Video.VideoCodecFrame.GetUserData answers the binding's own pointer and is not to be dereferenced.
$comment-skip-callback-lifetime: Three callbacks whose state has no derivable lifetime at all. gst_task_pool_push: whether the pushed function ever runs depends on the pool subclass and on a GLib thread start failure that queues the item all the same (gsttaskpool.c:100-120 and 440-467; gthreadpool.c:732 queues before it reports the failure), so an unprepared default pool sets an error and never invokes, a prepared one sets the same error and invokes later, and a shared pool answers NULL with no error - nothing in the return distinguishes them. Use Gst.Task or Gst.Object.CallAsync. gst_mini_object_set_qdata: the gir gives destroy no closure index, so the planner cannot pair it with data, and untyped per object storage has no typed projection - keep the state on the managed wrapper. gst_collect_pads_add_pad: the destroy notification is handed the GstCollectData block itself rather than a user_data pointer (GstBase-1.0.gir:11863 declares no closure parameter), and it only earns its keep when the caller over allocates that block, which a managed caller cannot.
$comment-skip-callback-value: Five callback carrying calls that are skipped on value rather than for a missing mechanism. gst_debug_remove_log_function matches the function to remove by pointer identity, and a managed delegate reaches native code through a thunk whose address is not the one that was installed, so the removal can never match; use the Gst.Global.DebugAddLogFunction return instead. gst_plugin_register_static is deprecated and superseded by gst_plugin_register_static_full, which is bound and does carry user data. gst_util_array_binary_search searches an untyped block by element size, which System.Array.BinarySearch already answers in managed code. gst_tracing_register_hook takes a GObject.Callback, the untyped placeholder of the tracer subsystem's varargs hooks, which is not a closure shape at all. gst_buffer_add_video_gl_texture_upload_meta is a deprecated OpenGL path that passes three callbacks through one closure index.
$comment-skip-meta-attachment: The enumerate, remove and serialize half of the metadata surface is hand written in Custom/BufferNative.cs and Custom/MetaNative.cs, and these entries state that intent in the ledger. gst_buffer_foreach_meta hands its callback a GstMeta** whose only meaningful write is NULL (gstbuffer.c:gst_buffer_foreach_meta tests new == NULL and discards any other pointer the callback stores), which is a keep/remove/stop decision rather than an inout parameter; no ArgumentKind describes it, and the trampoline also has to invalidate the wrapper of a removed item and re-throw a managed exception after the walk. gst_meta_serialize_simple takes a GByteArray* sink, of which the girs carry five occurrences in total, and its generated sibling Meta.Serialize(GstByteArrayInterface) is unreachable surface because Gst.ByteArrayInterface has no public constructor; the hand written Meta.Serialize() owns a GByteArray for the length of the call and answers a byte[]. gst_buffer_add_audio_meta sizes its offsets array by info->channels, a field of another parameter, which arrayOverrides cannot redirect to (it only names another parameter). gst_buffer_iterate_meta and gst_buffer_iterate_meta_filtered are introspectable='0' in the gir and never reach the classifier, so they get no entry here that the ledger could show; Gst.Buffer.IterateMeta imports the first by hand and does the filtering of the second in managed code.
$comment-skip-aggregate-params: gst_meta_api_type_aggregate_params takes GstStructure** and the gir declares GstStructure*, so the shipped Meta.ApiTypeAggregateParams passed a live structure where the library writes a pointer: the in-tree aggregator (gstvideometa.c:gst_video_meta_api_params_aggregator, registered at :202) assigns *aggregated_params on every path and never reads it, so each historical call overwrote the first eight bytes - the GType header - of the caller's own GstStructure and leaked the copy it had just made. The correction cannot be spelled as an annotationOverride: MarshalPlanner.OverriddenDirection accepts an out direction only for a pointer to a plain structure, to a GValue, to a scalar or to an enumeration, and GstStructure is a boxed record, so the entry would be reported as GEN0017 and ignored. The call is therefore skipped and written by hand, with the out parameter it always had and with the shipped signature kept beside it as an [Obsolete] bridge that throws: the parameter is passed by reference now, which is a binary break the package validation baseline does not see (it compares member signatures without the ref kind), and the 1.28.x promise is what keeps the old overload alive rather than the gate. gst_meta_api_type_set_params_aggregator is skipped with it: its callback typedef GstAllocationMetaParamsAggregator carries the same GstStructure** with no direction attribute at all, and MarshalPlanner.PlanCallbackCore rejects any callback parameter whose gir direction is not 'in' before an override is consulted - and MarshalPlanner.IsPointerToHandlePointer now refuses that GstStructure** ahead of the direction test in any case, because two stars over a boxed record is the pointer to a handle pointer shape, which is refused for a callback argument and for a signal argument as well as for an in parameter - so neither half of that pair is expressible today. It is meta authorship in any case - the aggregator is only useful to code that registers a new meta API type - and stays deferred with gst_meta_register and gst_meta_info_new. Both annotation faults are on the upstream report backlog.
$comment-skip-slaving-callback: gst_audio_base_sink_set_custom_slaving_callback is hand bound in src/GstSharp.Net.Audio/Custom/AudioBaseSink.cs. Its callback type GstAudioBaseSinkCustomSlavingCallback carries a GstClockTimeDiff *requested_skew, which is the whole point of the callback - gstaudiobasesink.c:1290-1294 passes the address of a local initialised to 0 and reads it back at :1302 and :1328 to move the playout pointer - and the gir types it as the bare gint64 with the star in the c:type alone. The generated trampoline therefore handed the delegate the pointer value itself as a long, so the skew could never be requested and the number the handler saw was an address; on a discontinuity, where gstaudiobasesink.c:769-777 passes NULL with GST_CLOCK_TIME_NONE for both clock times, it arrived as 0. MarshalPlanner.IsPointerToScalar refuses that parameter now, which takes the whole callback type and its trampoline out of the generated surface, so the delegate is re-declared by hand beside the setter the way Gst.BusSyncHandler is. The hand written surface is a handler that returns the requested skew, a trampoline that writes the return through the pointer when it is not NULL, SetCustomSlavingCallback and a ClearCustomSlavingCallback that passes NULL, which C documents as behaving like GST_AUDIO_BASE_SINK_SLAVE_NONE. The shipped delegate and the shipped setter overload are kept beside them as [Obsolete] bridges. The C setter at :761-765 overwrites the callback, the user data and the destroy notification without running the previous notification - only dispose does, at :315-316 - and the trio is read unlocked at :1292-1294, so a second call leaks the previous handle and can race an invocation that is already in flight; freeing it is not this binding's to do and is left where C leaves it.
$comment-skip-texture-upload: gst_video_gl_texture_upload_meta_upload is hand bound in src/GstSharp.Net.Video/Custom/VideoGLTextureUploadMeta.cs. The C function takes a guint texture_id[4] and forwards the block to the upload vfunc of the metadata item (gstvideometa.c:1284-1289), while the gir types the parameter as a bare guint with the star in the c:type alone, so the shipped Upload(uint) passed one texture id by value where the library dereferences an array of four: the vfunc it forwards the block to indexes texture_id[0..3], so it read four words at the address the identifier happened to name, if it survived the dereference at all. The hand written member takes a ReadOnlySpan<uint> instead, refuses a span shorter than the n_textures the item declares - gst_buffer_add_video_gl_texture_upload_meta bounds that count to 1..4 at gstvideometa.c:1253 - and copies it into a zero filled four element stack buffer whose address is what the C function is handed. The shipped overload is kept beside it as an [Obsolete] bridge that forwards a one element span, which is a working call for a single texture item and an ArgumentException for any other. No element of the 1.28 tree implements the upload vfunc and the add function is skipped as a deprecated closure path, so the metadata item can only arrive attached by a native element; there is nothing to exercise the call against in the test suite.

Listing one here changes nothing about what is generated: the symbol stays out for whatever reason already keeps it out - most of them are on the skip list above, the rest carry a signature or an annotation the generator does not bind - and the entry says that the generator must never offer a second way to call it. $comment-force-opaque-sdp: The payload structures of an SDP message are plain C structures that the library hands out by pointer, and every accessor of theirs takes or returns such a pointer. A plain structure is projected as a value type, which copies it, and the methods declared on it are dropped for exactly that reason, so the media, attribute, origin, connection, bandwidth, time, zone and key surface of the module is unreachable. Keeping the eight of them behind a pointer binds it: the wrapper addresses the storage the message owns, so a read sees the message and a write reaches it. As on every other opaque record, 'Free' and 'Uninit' are public on the wrappers; neither may be called on an instance that a message still owns.
$comment-force-opaque-transport: GstRTSPTransport is the same shape as the SDP payload structures and gets the same answer. It is a plain C structure the library hands out by pointer, gst_rtsp_transport_new allocates one and writes the address into an out parameter, and every accessor takes such a pointer, so projecting it as a value type drops as_text, free, get_media_type, get_manager and get_mime and leaves a structure whose destination and source fields are bare gchar pointers that no caller can read. Keeping it behind a pointer binds that surface and stops the two string fields from being offered as raw addresses. What stays unbound is init and parse, whose transport parameter is caller-allocates='1': a record bound behind a handle is one pointer wide, so the call would write a whole GstRTSPTransport past the end of what it is given, and they move to the CallerAllocates bucket exactly as gst_sdp_media_init and gst_sdp_message_init did. The range structures keep their value projection: GstRTSPRange is embedded by value four times in GstRTSPTransport and GstRTSPTime and GstRTSPTime2 are embedded in GstRTSPTimeRange, so forcing any of them behind a pointer would demote the structures that contain them, and their fields are plain integers that a copy reads correctly.
$comment-force-opaque-meta: A GstMeta lives inside the buffer that carries it. gst_buffer_get_meta and the typed gst_buffer_get_*_meta accessors hand out a pointer into the storage of that buffer, the lifetime of the metadata is the lifetime of the buffer, and a write to one of its fields is meant to reach the copy the buffer holds. A value projection can only ever snapshot it, and all three of the things a metadata item is for are lost by the copy: a read produces a structure that stopped tracking the buffer the moment it was taken, a write reaches a stack temporary that is discarded when the call returns, and the pointer identity that gst_buffer_remove_meta keys on is gone, which also takes with it any chance that what gst_buffer_iterate_meta and gst_buffer_foreach_meta walk over is the metadata of the buffer rather than a copy of it. That third one is not a prediction, it is the fault gst_buffer_remove_meta was skipped for above, which '$comment-skip-identity' records and which these entries cure. GstMeta itself is the header every metadata structure embeds by value as its first field, so the twenty two are forced together: keeping the header behind a pointer while the structures that carry it stay values, or the other way round, is the demotion the range structures of GstRTSPTransport are deliberately left by value to avoid. What the entries buy on their own is the correct foundation - a wrapper that addresses the metadata of the buffer instead of a copy of it - and the methods the gir declares on the records, which a plain structure drops. GstMetaInfo and GstVideoMeta are opaque already and are unaffected. The typed field accessors and the gst_buffer_add_*_meta, iterate and foreach attachment surface are purely additive on top of this shape and arrive later in the series.
$comment-force-opaque-static: A GstStaticCaps is a cache, not a value. gst_static_caps_get parses the string of the structure the first time it is asked and writes the GstCaps it built back through the pointer it was handed, under a lock, so that every later call on the same storage hands out that one caps; gst_static_caps_cleanup clears the field again. The identity of the storage is the whole contract, and a value projection can only snapshot it: the write back reaches a stack temporary that is discarded when the call returns, the cache the library meant to fill stays empty, and the reference the parse took is leaked once per call. GstStaticPadTemplate is the structure an element factory keeps in its own static storage, embeds a GstStaticCaps by value, and carries the same fault, so the two are forced together exactly as GstMeta and the structures that embed it are. The leak is not a prediction: Gst.Pad.NewFromStaticTemplate and Gst.PadTemplate.NewFromStaticPadTemplateWithGtype are the two shipped consumers, and both copied the structure into a local and handed the library the address of that copy, so every call reparsed the caps, leaked the reference the parse took and left the real cache of the factory untouched. Nothing is stranded by the change. The fields of the two are a cached pointer no caller may write and a name a caller has no way of supplying - a static pad template is declared in C by a macro no binding can reach - so neither structure was ever constructible from managed code, and what the value projection offered was the raw addresses of storage nobody could produce. Both also carry a registered GType and are boxed, which is the same statement about reference semantics from the other direction. Keeping them behind a pointer binds the four methods a plain structure drops: gst_static_caps_get and gst_static_caps_cleanup, gst_static_pad_template_get and gst_static_pad_template_get_caps. It also makes gst_element_factory_get_static_pad_templates reachable, which is what the change is for, because the pad templates of a factory could otherwise only be read by building an element first. That last one needed the planner to learn one thing as well - a returned GList may carry opaque records when the library keeps owning them, which the const GList of the factory does - and the rule is stated where it lives, on MarshalPlanner.PlanListReturn.
$comment-force-opaque-resampler: A GstVideoResampler owns four blocks of memory that only gst_video_resampler_clear can give back. gst_video_resampler_init allocates the offset, phase, n_taps and taps arrays for the sizes it is asked for and writes their addresses into the structure; clear frees all four and zeroes it again. A value projection makes that ownership copyable, and a public freely copyable value type that owns heap memory is a double free machine: every assignment, argument and return duplicates the four addresses, the first Clear on any copy releases the blocks that all of them still name, a second Clear frees them again and every read in between is a use after free. Nothing is stranded by the entry, because nothing today can reach either end of that lifecycle: a plain structure drops every method the gir declares on it, so init and clear were both in the UnsupportedSignature bucket and the record shipped as eight public fields with no member and no producer whatsoever. Behind a pointer the two bind, Clear() on the instance and Init(method, flags, n_phases, n_taps, shift, in_size, out_size, options) with the two enumerations of the module and the options GstStructure passed as the boxed wrapper it already is. They are not reachable from outside the assembly yet and are not meant to be: the wrapper of an opaque record has an internal constructor, and the producer of a resampler is storage the caller allocates, which the binding has no spelling for until the hand written scope that Gst.Buffer.Map and Gst.Base.Adapter.Map have is written for it. What the entry buys now is the shape that scope needs and the removal of a value type that hands out four raw addresses it also claims to own.
$comment-force-opaque-cd-track: The tags field of a GstAudioCdSrcTrack is a GstTagList the base class takes ownership of. gst_audio_cd_src_add_track is documented as doing a shallow copy of the structure and taking the reference of the taglist out of the caller's storage, so a single instance may be added exactly once and the caller must not release the tags afterwards. A value projection cannot express that: a copyable value type that owns a refcount duplicates the reference on every copy while the count stays where it was, so whichever copy is handed to the call decides the ownership of a reference every other copy still names. The structure was unusable in that projection anyway. Its tags field was emitted as a bare nint, and the binding hands out no address of a GstTagList that a caller could put there, so the one field the call exists to transfer was the one field no caller could set. What it is for is narrower still: the gir says the structure is only for use by subclasses, and its sole consumer is implementor API of GstAudioCdSrc, a base class this binding cannot yet be subclassed from. Behind a pointer the record is a wrapper with no member, and gst_audio_cd_src_add_track stays bound but takes that wrapper, which nothing outside the assembly can construct - the call is no longer reachable by accident and no longer offers a value type whose ownership contract it cannot keep. Producing a track belongs with the subclassing surface of GstAudioCdSrc once that exists.
$comment-force-opaque-timecode-config: GstVideoTimeCodeConfig carries a latest_daily_jam that is a GDateTime, which is refcounted, and gst_video_time_code_new is documented as stealing the reference the caller passes for it. That is the same statement the CD track entry above makes: a copyable value type cannot own a reference, because every copy names it and none of them can be said to hold it. Nothing is given up by the change, and this was checked rather than assumed. The girs mention the type in exactly one place other than its own declaration - the config field of GstVideoTimeCode - and no callable anywhere takes or returns one: gst_video_time_code_new, init, new_from_date_time and their _full variants all take fps_n, fps_d, latest_daily_jam and flags as separate arguments and never a config. GstVideoTimeCode is a boxed record, so it is wrapped by a class and exposes no public field, which means the config field is not part of the surface either; GstVideoTimeCodeMeta embeds a GstMeta and is already behind a pointer with it. So no member takes a config, no member hands one out, and the value projection was four public fields with no producer and no consumer. Behind a pointer the record has no member either - the gir declares no method on it - but the projection is the one the eventual accessor needs: reading the configuration of a time code has to address the structure the time code owns, so that the daily jam is the live GDateTime of that time code rather than a borrowed address snapshotted into a copy that took no reference on it.
$comment-rename-get-type: gst_rtsp_message_get_type reads the message kind out of a GstRTSPMessage, and its derived C# name is GetType, which every object already declares. The generator refuses the collision and skips the member, so the kind of a message would be unreadable; GetMessageType is the name the C# surface gives it. The type of the record itself is registered under gst_rtsp_msg_get_type and is unaffected. gst_rtcp_packet_get_type reads the packet kind out of a GstRTCPPacket and collides the same way; GetPacketType is its C# name. The record itself carries no GType at all - its gir record declares no glib:get-type - so the C name is not taken by anything else.
$comment-rename-commited: GESTimeline and GESTrack both emit their commit signal under the name 'commited', with one 't'. The typo is the API, since connecting to 'committed' connects to nothing, so the gir is right and only the C# name is corrected here. The signal name the generated code passes to GObject is the one of the gir; the rename reaches the event alone.
$comment-rename-digits: An enumeration member whose gir name starts with a digit has no legal C# spelling of its own, and the generator used to prepend a bare underscore to it. That underscore carries no meaning, and the names it produced were actively misleading: GST_RTSP_VERSION_1_0 arrived as RTSPVersion._10, which reads as ten and whose value is 16, GST_VIDEO_COLOR_RANGE_16_235 as VideoColorRange._16235, which reads as one number where the C name states two, GST_VIDEO_ORIENTATION_90R as VideoOrientationMethod._90r, and the nine aspect ratio codes of GstVideoAFDValue as _169Letter43Center and its like, where both ratios of the code have run into single numbers. All of them are renamed here so that the C# name states what the C name states. The leading letter or word is the one the underscore stood in for - V for a protocol version, Range for a sample range, Rotate for a rotation, Ratio for an aspect ratio code - and an underscore inside the name separates the two numbers of a ratio, so 16_9 reads as 16:9 exactly as GST_VIDEO_AFD_16_9_TOP_ALIGNED spells it and 16_235 as the [16..235] range its documentation describes. GreaterThan16_9 is renamed for that second half alone: its derived name GreaterThan169 needs no escape and was legal C#, but it sits in the same enumeration as Ratio16_9TopAligned and has to spell its ratio the same way. The generator no longer prepends an underscore for an enumeration member at all: a member whose derived name still starts with a digit fails the run with GEN0016, which names the member and the key to add here, so a gir refresh that introduces one cannot ship a name like this again. GST_RTP_PAYLOAD_1016 is the same case with a different answer: its value is 1, so Pt1016 or Payload1016 would read as payload type 1016, exactly the misreading RTSPVersion._10 was renamed away from. RFC 3551, the standard this enumeration follows, defines payload type 1 as the FS-1016 CELP codec, so the member is Fs1016 and the string twin GST_RTP_PAYLOAD_1016_STRING stays the literal "1" the header spells.
$comment-rename-control-binding-name: GstControlBinding installs a construct-only "name" property of its own that holds the name of the CONTROLLED PROPERTY - gstcontrolbinding.c fills binding->name from it in set_property and hands it back in get_property, and gst_control_binding_constructed looks that name up with g_object_class_find_property on the object the binding was constructed for, keeping the pspec it finds when that property is writable, controllable and not construct-only. gst_object_add_control_binding does not resolve anything: it refuses a binding whose pspec stayed NULL, and uses binding->name to find the binding of the same property it replaces. It is not the name of the binding object: GstObject already declares "name", gst_object_get_name reads it and Gst.Object.Name binds it. A generated Name would therefore hide an inherited member of the same name with entirely different semantics, which is why the value backed shape skips such a property outright; the rename is what binds it instead, under the name that says which of the two it is. The key is the GObject spelling of a property, which is what NameMapper.PropertyName looks the rename up under.
$comment-nullable-callbacks: A callback parameter without a nullable annotation is a value the C contract promises, and the emitted delegate spells it as non-null so that a handler does not have to null check what cannot be null. These four are the places where the gir promises a value the library does not always pass, and each is corrected here rather than by blanket-nullabling every handle a callback receives. The three caps callbacks read their features with gst_caps_get_features_unchecked, which is the accessor that does not materialise them: an entry that carries none hands the callback a NULL, which the gir states for gst_caps_get_features - its return value is nullable - and omits on the callbacks that see the same pointer. GstLogFunction is the prototype of gst_debug_log_default, and every one of gst_debug_log, gst_debug_log_valist, gst_debug_log_literal, gst_debug_log_default and gst_debug_log_get_line annotates its object parameter nullable: logging without an object is what GST_DEBUG does when it is not given one, so most log lines arrive with none. Keys are the c:type of the callback, because a callback carries no c:identifier.
$comment-direction-writeback: The gir has one spelling for a pointer to a plain structure whether the C function reads it or fills it: a bare 'GstVideoAlignment*' with no direction attribute on it. The planner passes such a parameter by value - the member copies the argument into a local and hands the address of that local over - which is right for the ones that are read and silently wrong for the ones that are written, because the copy the call filled in is discarded when the member returns. These entries name the written ones. gst_buffer_pool_config_get_video_alignment is a getter whose whole output is that structure, so what shipped was a member that parsed the alignment out of the configuration, threw it away and answered TRUE: a pure information sink, and there is no other way of reading the alignment of a pool configuration. gst_video_info_align and gst_video_info_align_full read the alignment the caller asks for and write back the padding they had to raise to satisfy the stride alignment - the C documentation says so in as many words, and the XML documentation the generator copies onto the members promised it while the code discarded it - which breaks the negotiation sequence those calls exist for, where the padding that comes back out of align is what goes into gst_buffer_pool_config_set_video_alignment. gst_video_meta_map fills the GstMapInfo the caller allocates exactly as gst_buffer_map does, and the gir spells the two differently for no reason: gst_buffer_map carries direction='out' caller-allocates='1' and gst_video_meta_map carries nothing, so Map returned a mapping the caller could not see. Its unmap is 'ref' rather than 'in' because it has to be handed the info that map wrote and because meta->map and meta->unmap are function pointers of the metadata item that any element may replace, so what runs on the other side of the call is not one fixed implementation. gst_buffer_unmap and gst_memory_unmap are the deliberate exceptions: their parameter is non-const as well, but the implementation behind them is fixed - a memory unmap through the allocator of the block - and reads the info without writing it, so passing the value is correct there and they keep the signature they shipped with. The correction is refused for anything but a pointer to a plain structure, to a GValue, to a scalar or to an enumeration; a pointer to a scalar is what the RTCP XR readers of $comment-xr-out are corrected with and a pointer to an enumeration is what the two SDES entry readers of $comment-sdes-out are corrected with, while a handle, a string or an array still has an out projection of its own.
$comment-direction-poll: The whole gst_poll file descriptor family takes a 'GstPollFD*' the library keeps state in. GstPollFD carries a private 'idx' beside the descriptor, which is the position of the descriptor inside the set: gst_poll_add_fd writes it after appending, and the lookup every other call starts with reads it as a hint, verifies it against the descriptor it names and rewrites it when the hint was stale. Passing a copy hands that state to a stack temporary that the member discards, so the cache the library maintains in the caller's structure is thrown away once per call and nothing the caller holds ever learns the index it was given. Every one of the eleven is turned into a 'ref' for it, which is the storage the C function was written to be handed. One gap stays and is not this correction's to close: GST_POLL_FD_INIT initialises idx to -1 and the gir marks the field private, so a default-constructed Gst.PollFD starts with an idx of 0 rather than -1. The lookup validates the hint against the descriptor before it trusts it, so a wrong index is recovered from rather than acted on. Gst.PollFD.Init, which the record emitter now binds along with the other methods of a plain structure, is the call that sets the descriptor and the index the way GST_POLL_FD_INIT does; a default-constructed value still starts with an idx of 0, so a caller that means the initialised state calls Init on a variable of its own.
$comment-fixed-arrays: Two members pass a pointer to one element where the C function unconditionally writes four of them: GST_VIDEO_MAX_PLANES for the one and GST_VIDEO_MAX_COMPONENTS for the other. The gir describes both as a pointer to a single value - 'gsize*' and 'gint*', direction out - so the planner emitted 'out nuint' and 'out int', and every call wrote 24 and 12 bytes past the end of the local the member had allocated: the caller's stack frame, corrupted on every single call, with the damage landing on whatever the compiler had put beside that local. gst_video_info_align_full fills the aligned size of each of the four planes and gst_video_format_info_component fills the component numbers packed in one plane, terminated by a -1 when the plane carries fewer than four. The size is a fact about the C implementation that no gir annotation carries, so it is stated here; the parameter is then planned as an out of an [InlineArray] struct of that length, nested in the declaring type and named after the parameter, so the storage is the size the callee writes, the caller cannot supply less, and nothing is allocated per call.
$comment-transfer-prepare-read: gst_audio_ring_buffer_prepare_read hands out a pointer into the ring buffer's own segment memory - 'a pointer to memory where the data from segment can be found', in the words of its C documentation, borrowed for as long as the buffer stays acquired. The gir annotates the out parameter transfer-ownership='full', which is the auto-annotation default for an out pointer and wrong here, and the generated member took it literally: it copied the bytes out, correctly, and then handed the borrowed interior pointer to g_free, corrupting the heap on every successful call. The override states the borrow; the member keeps copying, which is the right projection of memory whose lifetime belongs to the device thread.
$comment-direction-range: Two annotations of the GstRTSPRange functions that do not describe the C implementation, verified against GStreamer 1.28.6. gst_rtsp_range_convert_units is documented as converting the range in place, and it does: it rewrites range->unit and both ends of range->min and range->max, yet its parameter carries no direction attribute, so the planner would pass a copy the member throws away and the caller would see nothing change. It is re-planned as 'ref'. gst_rtsp_range_to_string states a non-nullable return while the C function answers NULL for a unit its switch does not know, which the planner would turn into an InvalidOperationException on a value a caller can legitimately hold. Both gir lies go to the upstream report backlog.
$comment-direction-value-dest: Four GValue destinations whose gir direction does not describe the C function, verified against GStreamer 1.28.6. gst_value_deserialize opens with a G_IS_VALUE guard on dest and picks its parser by G_VALUE_TYPE(dest) (gstvalue.c:7340-7342), and gst_util_set_value_from_string reads G_VALUE_TYPE(value) and delegates to that same deserialize (gstutils.c:162-164) - both are annotated direction='out' caller-allocates='1', which the planner projects as storage the member zeroes, so every call would fail the type check before parsing anything; they are re-planned as 'ref', the pre-initialized destination the parser table needs. gst_value_deserialize_with_pspec (1.20) is the third of that shape and the one this correction was written for: it is annotated direction='out' caller-allocates='1' while gstvalue.c:7391 opens with g_return_val_if_fail (G_IS_VALUE (dest), FALSE), reads G_VALUE_TYPE (dest) to pick the parser and, when a pspec is given, requires that type to equal G_PARAM_SPEC_VALUE_TYPE (pspec) (gstvalue.c:7393-7395), so a zeroed destination fails before anything is parsed; it becomes 'ref' like its two siblings. gst_value_fixate is the opposite fault: its dest carries no direction at all, so it would land in the initialized-ref shape, while the C function g_value_inits dest on every branch (gstvalue.c:7510-7600) and a pre-initialized dest would g_critical; it is the true out that no annotation states. gst_value_fraction_multiply and gst_value_fraction_subtract are the deliberate exceptions and get no entry: their gir already spells direction=in on a non-const pointer, which is the 'ref' projection, and their product/dest really must arrive initialized to GST_TYPE_FRACTION.
$comment-transfer-intersect-dest: gst_value_intersect annotates dest transfer-ownership='full' while gst_value_union and gst_value_subtract - the same caller allocated dest in the same file - say 'none'. All three place caller owned contents in dest on TRUE (gstvalue.c:6975-6979, 7113 and 6818 at 1.28.6), so the gir disagrees with itself rather than with the code. The generated out projection of a caller allocated GValue does not key on transfer - the caller owns the contents and disposes them in every shape - so the override changes no emitted byte today; it is stated so the three siblings read identically and a future transfer keyed rule cannot split them.
$comment-discard-init-return: gst_value_array_init and gst_value_list_init return the very GValue pointer they were handed - 'The #GValue structure that has been passed in', in the words of their own gir - as a convenience for chaining in C. The planner projects a transfer-none GValue return as a deep copy the caller owns, so binding it would copy a list that was just initialized empty into a second value the caller then has to dispose, for a result it already holds. The return is dropped instead and the members are void, which is what a C caller of gst_value_list_init does with it.
$comment-direction-sdp-media: The gir of gst_sdp_media_set_media_from_caps and of gst_sdp_media_add_media_from_structure calls their media parameter a caller allocated out. It is not one: gstsdpmessage.c:2115 frees the media string that is already in the structure before it writes the new one, and gst_sdp_media_add_format at :148-153 appends to media->fmts, so both functions require a GstSDPMedia that gst_sdp_media_new or gst_sdp_media_init has initialised and would walk uninitialised storage otherwise. The override corrects the parameter onto an in parameter that transfers nothing, which is what the C functions take; the annotation is an upstream bug and is on the report backlog.
$comment-nullable-daily-jam: gst_video_time_code_new and gst_buffer_add_video_time_code_meta_full both document @latest_daily_jam as (allow-none) in their C comments - gstvideotimecode.c:634 and gstvideometa.c:1698 at 1.28.6 - and both hand the pointer straight to gst_video_time_code_init (gstvideotimecode.c:651-660, gstvideometa.c:1727), which refs it when it is non-NULL and stores NULL otherwise (gstvideotimecode.c:855-858). That is the same contract the gir states for gst_video_time_code_init itself; the scanner dropped the annotation on the two callers only. The dt family - gst_video_time_code_new_from_date_time, _full and the two init_from_date_time siblings - gets no entry: gst_video_time_code_init_from_date_time_full opens with g_return_val_if_fail (dt != NULL, FALSE) (gstvideotimecode.c:282) and every one of them funnels into it, so the gir is right there. Both corrections go to the upstream report backlog.
$comment-strv-nullability: Nine string arrays whose gir says NULL is impossible and whose C says otherwise. Returns: gst_debug_ring_buffer_logger_get_logs answers NULL for a logger that was never installed and its disabled build is a NULL stub (gstinfo.c:4607, :4716); gst_element_factory_get_uri_protocols hands back factory->uri_protocols, which is NULL for every factory that is not a URI handler (gstelementfactory.c:997-1002); gst_meta_api_type_get_tags returns NULL for an api registered with an empty tag list (gstmeta.c:410-421); gst_preset_get_preset_names and gst_preset_get_property_names return NULL from the no_presets and no_groups paths of the default implementation (gstpreset.c:518-566, :570-595); gst_discoverer_info_get_missing_elements_installer_details returns NULL unless the result is MISSING_PLUGINS (gstdiscoverer-types.c:1190-1200). Parameters: gst_device_has_classesv returns TRUE for a NULL class list (gstdevice.c:357-365) and the repeat list of gst_sdp_message_add_time and gst_sdp_time_set is guarded with if (repeat) before it is walked (gstsdpmessage.c:1277-1283, :1386, and the internal caller at :403-418). The six return entries state a fact the projection already spells - an ArgumentKind.Strv return is string[]? whatever the gir claims - so they read as documentation today and keep the correction addressable if that ever narrows; the three parameter entries decide the emitted signature. All nine are on the upstream report backlog.
$comment-scope-collect-pads: The GstCollectPads setters annotate their function (scope call), which says the library is done with it when the setter returns. It is not: gst_collect_pads_set_function stores func and user_data in pads->priv (gstcollectpads.c:297-327) and gst_collect_pads_check_collected calls them from the streaming thread long afterwards, reading the pointers under the object lock and invoking outside it (gstcollectpads.c:1316-1317), which also rules out freeing the previous state when the function is replaced. The five members shipped with a finally that freed the GCHandle as the setter returned, so every collected buffer read a freed handle. The scope is corrected to forever: the state is never released, one handle is leaked per call, and the generated documentation says so. gst_collect_pads_set_buffer_function and gst_collect_pads_set_clip_function carry the same wrong annotation and get no entry because neither is bindable today - the first hands the callback a buffer with transfer-ownership='full' and the second an out parameter - and an entry that corrects nothing would be dead. All seven annotations are on the upstream report backlog.
$comment-nullable-error-loading-asset: The gir gives @error no nullable annotation although its own doc says it 'might be %NULL'. It can be: ges_project_create_asset_sync emits the signal with *error (ges-project.c:1012) straight from ges_asset_request, which returns a NULL asset without ever setting the error in its ASSET_INITIALIZING, broken ASSET_PROXIED, failed ASSET_NEEDS_RELOAD, ASSET_INITIALIZED_WITH_ERROR-with-NULL-error and default arms and in the no-init branch (ges-asset.c:1286, 1293, 1305, 1312, 1316, 1337-1338). On that path ges_project_try_updating_id trips its own g_return_val_if_fail and the emission carries a NULL GError. The other five GError signals need no correction: GstDiscoverer::discovered and GESDiscovererManager::discovered are already nullable, and GESProject::error-loading, GESProject::missing-uri and GstWebRTCDataChannel::on-error are each guarded non-NULL at their sole emit site (ges-project.c:832-835, ges-project.c:737-755, datachannel.c:453-463). Reported upstream.
$comment-obsolete-get-transports: gst_rtsp_extension_get_transports takes a gchar** the implementation writes the transport string into, and the gir declares it as a plain utf8 with no direction, so the member that shipped in 1.28.0 takes a string, copies it into a temporary UTF-8 buffer and hands the library the address of that buffer: the g_strdup an extension writes there lands in a temporary the member discards and leaks. The base function never touches the pointer itself (gst-plugins-base/gst-libs/gst/rtsp/gstrtspextension.c:169-180) - it returns GST_RTSP_OK and calls the vfunc only where an extension implements one - so the caller pre-initialises the destination, which gst_rtspsrc_create_transports_string does at gst-plugins-good/gst/rtsp/gstrtspsrc.c:7615 before chaining the extensions, and owns whatever comes back: it is freed with g_free at :8216, :8229 and :8239 and handed to gst_rtsp_message_take_header at :8255. Correcting the parameter to an out would reshape a published member, which the 1.28.x promise does not allow, so the working shape is hand written beside it as Gst.Rtsp.RTSPExtensionExtensions.GetTransports(..., out string?) in src/GstSharp.Net.Rtsp/Custom/RTSPExtensionExtensions.cs and the generated member is marked here. The correction of the parameter itself belongs to 1.30, where the generated member takes the out parameter and this entry goes away with the hand written sibling. The missing direction annotation is on the upstream report backlog.
$comment-rename-map-buffer: gst_rtp_buffer_map and gst_rtcp_buffer_map fill a caller allocated GstRTPBuffer or GstRTCPBuffer, and their derived C# name is Map, which the accessor of the GstMapInfo field named map that both records carry already holds. The generator refuses the collision and skips the member, which would leave the one call without which nothing else on either record can be used unbound. MapBuffer is the name the C# surface gives them - it says which of the two things the member maps - and the field keeps Map.
$comment-direction-rtcp-out: Three parameters the RTCP functions fill and the gir spells as a bare pointer with no direction at all, verified against GStreamer 1.28.6. gst_rtcp_buffer_map writes the whole GstRTCPBuffer it is handed: gstrtcpbuffer.c:310 requires the buffer field to arrive NULL, which the default initialised temporary of the generated member guarantees, and :314-315 then write the structure. gst_rtcp_buffer_get_first_packet (:479-483) and gst_rtcp_buffer_add_packet (:557, :592) fill the GstRTCPPacket they are handed and read nothing out of it. Without the correction the record would be passed by value, the result of the call thrown away and, for the map, the mapping leaked.
$comment-xr-out: The fifty one out parameters of the eighteen gst_rtcp_packet_xr_get_* readers of an extended report block. Every one of the readers answers through pointers the C function writes before it returns TRUE - gstrtcpbuffer.h:586-667 declares them all as guintN * or gboolean *, and each body writes through every pointer it was given, skipping only the ones the caller passed NULL for, as gst_rtcp_packet_xr_get_rrt does at gstrtcpbuffer.c:3104-3105 and gst_rtcp_packet_xr_get_summary_ttl at :3360-3375 - while the gir types each parameter as the bare scalar the pointer points at, with the star in the c:type alone and no direction attribute on it. Generated from that shape the member would pass the value where the C function writes through the address, so calling one would corrupt memory at a location the caller never chose, and the eighteen readers were skipped for it. A direction override reaches them: the planner re-plans a pointer to a scalar as an out parameter the way it already does a pointer to a plain structure and to a GValue, the star of the c:type being the evidence that the C function writes through it. The missing direction annotations are on the upstream report backlog.
$comment-sdes-out: The 'type' of gst_rtcp_packet_sdes_get_entry and of gst_rtcp_packet_sdes_copy_entry is the entry type the packet carries and not one the caller states. The C bodies write through it - gstrtcpbuffer.c:1539 is 'if (type) *type = item_type;' inside gst_rtcp_packet_sdes_get_entry, and gst_rtcp_packet_sdes_copy_entry at :1573 forwards the pointer it was handed to that very call - while the gir types the parameter as the bare 'RTCPSDESType' with the star in the c:type alone and no direction attribute on it, exactly as it does for the XR readers above. Generated from that shape the member took an RTCPSDESType the caller had to invent and handed its value to a function that dereferences it, so the entry type was unreadable and the call wrote through whatever the value happened to be. The direction override reaches an enumeration the same way it reaches a scalar: the out projection is a local of the underlying integer and the member converts it back. The 'len' and 'data' parameters beside it are annotated correctly and are untouched. The missing direction annotations are on the upstream report backlog.

$comment-array-overrides: Corrections of an <array> the gir already spells, keyed like annotationOverrides. $comment-return-types: The gir spells the factory of a subclass with the return type of its base, so gst_pipeline_new returns a GstElement even though it only ever constructs a GstPipeline. The override narrows the wrapper onto the declaring type, which is the one the C implementation is known to build. The three network clock factories are the same shape with one wrinkle: gst_net_client_clock_new keeps a cache of clocks, which gst_net_client_clock_deinit is documented as clearing, so what it returns is not always freshly built. It is still an instance of the declaring type or of something below it, and the wrapper is created from the real type of the instance rather than from the declared one, so the narrowing holds either way.
$comment-field-skips: Record fields that carry API in C and are answered by something other than an accessor of their own, keyed by the c:type of the record and the gir name of the field. A field of a reserved ABI union is addressed by the record it grows, with the union and the structure inside it transparent, the same way its accessor would be named. The entry keeps the field out of the field ledger of the skip report and keeps the generator from emitting an accessor for it, which is what makes it the answer to a name a hand written member already carries. Exactly one of 'exposedBy' and 'handBound' has to be stated, and the check is exclusive; a key that matches no field of an emitted record, an entry that states neither, and an entry that states both are all reported as GEN0025.
$comment-field-skip-flow-ret: GstPadProbeInfo.flow_ret is the value a blocking probe hands back to the pad, and gst_pad_probe_info_get_flow_return reads that very field through a C function; both halves of the pair are generated, as PadProbeInfo.GetFlowReturn and .SetFlowReturn. An accessor over the mirror would be a second spelling of one value, and the C function is the half that stays right if the field ever moves inside the union.

$comment-field-annotations: What no gir annotation carries about a record field, keyed the way 'fieldSkips' is. Three corrections are read. 'nullable: false' says the field never holds the null pointer, which a gir cannot spell on a <field> at all, and emits the accessor of it non nullable. 'name' is the stem the member that reads the field is named after, in place of the one the field name derives, and the rule that decides between a property and a Get method works on it unchanged. 'accessor: false' holds the field back from the accessors: the pointer stays on the mirror and the field stays on the ledger under its own shape, and it excludes the other two, which may be stated together. A key that matches no field an accessor would be emitted for, an entry that states nothing or only the default, an empty name and a name the field derives anyway are all reported as GEN0026. Every citation below is relative to the GStreamer 1.28 monorepo, subprojects/.
$comment-field-annotation-accessor: Four reasons hold a field back below, and each entry states its own. One is a pointer the header keeps to the implementation of the structure, where the copy the boxed wrapper takes aliases what the owner frees. One is storage the user fills and hands to the library, which takes it over and would refuse to write a list a reference of ours made unwritable. Six are the header a derived record embeds, whose wrapper the surface has no way of reaching. One is held out with the rest of backlog #20. A field newer than the support floor is refused by the generator rather than by an entry here: the structure an older library allocates does not hold it, so no overlay may lift that.
$comment-field-annotation-mikey-pt: The pt of a derived MIKEY payload is the GstMIKEYPayload header every variant carries first (gst-plugins-base/gst-libs/gst/sdp/gstmikey.h:159-166), and the header is a GstMiniObject whose len is the size of the derived payload (gstmikey.c:852). An accessor would hand out a reference to the whole payload under the name of its header, and the direction a reader needs is the other one: from the payload to the variant, which is a cast the binding does not have. The six derived wrappers carry no public producer either, so the accessor would be surface nothing reaches. gst_mikey_payload_copy runs the copy function gst_mikey_payload_new selected for the type (gstmikey.c:794-856), and that function copies the whole derived payload: for KEMAC, a g_memdup2 of sizeof(GstMIKEYPayloadKEMAC) followed by a copy of every sub payload (gstmikey.c:157-170). That is what makes a header only copy of one a corrupt mini object.
